Joint Comments of the New York State Department of Health and the New York State Department of Veterans’ Services
Introduction
The U.S. Department of Veteran’s Affairs (VA) amended its medical benefits package on September 9, 2022 to permit pregnant beneficiaries of the Veterans and Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA) to access abortion services when the life or the health of the pregnant Veteran would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term, or if the pregnancy resulted from an act of rape or incest.
CHAMPVA regulations were also changed in 2022 to permit abortion counseling, as a part of a comprehensive counseling of pregnancy options, for Veterans, spouses, and dependents to allow patients to make informed decisions about their care. This brought Veteran and CHAMPVA care in line with Tricare, which already had these provisions for abortion care and abortion counseling.1 The New York State Department of Health and the Department of Veterans Services (the Departments) write to express their joint opposition to the proposed rule.
Impacts of the Proposed Rule
The VA now proposes rule RIN 2900-AS31, which would reinstate pre-2022 full exclusions on abortions and abortion counseling, claiming this will "ensure that VA provides only needed medical services to our nation's heroes and their families." 
The number of impacted Veterans and family members is substantial. It is estimated that in the United States, there are more than two-million-woman Veterans2 and thousands of transgender men and non-binary Veterans3 who would be eligible for abortion care. There are 700,000 family members eligible for CHAMPVA that would also be impacted.4  
Further, VA Secretary Doug Collins has stated repeatedly that his top priority is the prevention of Veteran suicide. This priority is undermined with this proposed regulatory change. In December 2022, for instance, the peer-reviewed journal JAMA Psychiatry published a longitudinal study verifying that restricting abortion access is linked to increased suicide risk for women of reproductive age.5  Thus, if Secretary Collins truly wishes to prioritize the prevention of Veteran suicide, then abortion care and counseling is indeed scientifically proven to be a "needed medical services to our nation's heroes and their families."6  
It is important to note that abortion care and counseling is recognized as medical care by leading medical bodies, including the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Removing the abortion care and counseling provision for Veterans and CHAMPVA would create confusion among veterans and their families and create uneven access to care based on where in the country veterans live. Access to care for those who have given so much to our country should not be dependent on state lines; all veterans deserve access to quality, affordable medical care.
Rape Provision
The current medical benefits package excludes abortions, except in cases of rape and incest and health of the pregnant person. Women Veterans experiencing homelessness are among the most at-risk populations for sexual assault. Furthermore, during their service one in three female veterans report experiencing sexual assault.7 When examining female Veterans who are unhoused, up to 40% have experienced military sexual trauma.8 
Additionally, female Veterans experienced unsheltered homelessness at a higher rate than sheltered homelessness (12% vs 9%), meaning they are more likely to spend time on the street and not in a shelter.9 Because these female Veterans experiencing homelessness have an increased risk that they become victims of sexual violence,10 this would mean they could need abortion care under the current medical regulations, but would be turned away from care if these medical regulations were changed.
Health of the Pregnant Person Provision
There are inherent risks to military family and spouses, as well as female Veterans if abortion access is prohibited and pregnancies are forced to progress: the risk to the health of the pregnant person.  Pregnancies have inherent risks, with 700 people dying each year in the US from pregnancy-related conditions and 50,000 people having short- or long-term health complications from their pregnancy or birth.11   This rule could impede treatment for ectopic pregnancy, for example. These pregnancies are never viable and can result in severe complications, including death, if not treated urgently.
If Veterans and CHAMPVA recipients are denied abortion care services when the life or the health of the pregnant person would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term, this would result in severe complications or death.  Even a delay in seeking care can be devastating.  The change in medical regulations puts Veterans and their dependents at risk.
Conclusion 
Abortion care is a critical component of healthcare.12,13,14 Both the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society of Maternal-Fetal Medicine oppose policies that limit abortion access and/or a healthcare providers ability to counsel patients.13,14 The change in these medical regulations stand in stark contrast to these recommendations. 
Many Veterans fought for years to eliminate these long-standing barriers at Veterans Health Administration facilities. To have them reinstated now is a step backward. Veterans Health Administration is the largest integrated healthcare network in the nation, and should prioritize the provision of this critical counseling and care.
The New York State Department of Health and the New York State Department of Veterans Services appreciates VA’s consideration of our comments on this Proposed Rule and urges the agency to keep the medical benefits package as it is currently and not revert back to where they were before September 8, 2022.   If changes are made, it will cause undue harm to the Veterans and families of Veterans on CHAMPVA across the country. 
If you require additional information about the issues raised in these comments, please contact Associate Commissioner of Governmental and External Affairs Alyssa DeRosa, at alyssa.derosa@health.ny.gov.
